section.title: Paul and the False Apostles
section.sectionRationale: Paul's defense sharpens into open warning. Like a father who has betrothed his daughter to one husband, he is jealous with a godly jealousy to present the Corinthian church as a pure virgin to Christ, and he fears they are being seduced from their simple devotion to Him. He unmasks the intruders who preach a different Jesus as false apostles, deceitful workers, servants of the Satan who masquerades as an angel of light.
section.thesis: Godly jealousy longs to keep the church in pure and sincere devotion to Christ alone; those who preach another Jesus, a different spirit, and a different gospel are not superior apostles but false apostles and deceitful workers, servants of Satan disguised as servants of righteousness, whose end will match their deeds.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the church betrothed as a pure virgin to Christ and Paul's fear of a second Eve; his preaching free of charge over against the super-apostles; and the unmasking of the false apostles as Satan's servants in disguise.

units.label: Betrothed to one husband
units.note: as Eve was deceived, so your minds may be led astray

verses.text: I hope you will put up with a little of my foolishness, but you are already doing that.
I am jealous for you with a godly {{zelos|jealousy}}. For I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your {{haplotes|simple and pure devotion}} to Christ.

For if someone comes and proclaims a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit than the One you received, or a different gospel than the one you accepted, you put up with it very easily.

units.label: Preaching free of charge
units.note: in no way inferior to the super-apostles

verses.text: I consider myself in no way inferior to those “super-apostles.”
Although I am not a polished speaker, I am certainly not lacking in knowledge. We have made this clear to you in every way possible.
Was it a sin for me to humble myself in order to exalt you, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?
I robbed other churches by accepting their support in order to serve you.

And when I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs. I have refrained from being a burden to you in any way, and I will continue to do so.
As surely as the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!

units.label: Masquerading as apostles
units.note: Satan disguised as an angel of light

verses.text: But I will keep on doing what I am doing, in order to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast.
For such men are {{pseudapostolos|false apostles}}, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ.
And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.
It is not surprising, then, if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their actions.

zelos.gloss: Zeal, ardor, or jealousy. The word can be a sin, envious rivalry, or a holy passion; Paul specifies a godly jealousy, a jealousy that belongs to God. Like a father guarding his betrothed daughter, Paul burns with the same jealous love that God has for His covenant people. It is not petty possessiveness but a righteous longing that the church be kept wholly for Christ, her one true husband.

haplotes.gloss: Simplicity, singleness, sincerity. It describes an undivided heart, a devotion to Christ that is pure and uncomplicated by rival loyalties. Paul fears the Corinthians will be lured away from this single-hearted attachment to Christ, just as Eve was drawn from trusting God's word. The word warns that the gospel can be lost not only by open denial but by the subtle diluting of wholehearted love for the Savior.

pseudapostolos.gloss: A false apostle, a counterfeit sent one. Paul coins a blunt term for the intruders who pose as apostles of Christ but serve another master. However impressive their claims, they are deceitful workers whose true allegiance is to Satan, who disguises himself as an angel of light. The word strips away the mask: they are not merely mistaken teachers but frauds whose end will match their deeds.

basic.context: Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with a little foolishness as he defends himself. He writes as a spiritual father who betrothed the church to one husband, Christ, and now fears she is being seduced away, as Eve was deceived by the serpent. Rival teachers, whom he sarcastically calls super-apostles, have won a hearing by preaching a different Jesus. Paul unmasks them as false apostles and servants of Satan disguised as servants of righteousness.
basic.hermeneutics: This is impassioned pastoral warning, not calm exposition. Read the marriage imagery of verses 2 to 3 as the key: the church is engaged to Christ, and any teaching that draws her from single-hearted devotion to Him is spiritual adultery. Paul's refusal to take pay from Corinth, verses 7 to 11, is part of the argument, distinguishing him from the money-motivated intruders.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul burns with zelos, a godly jealousy, to keep the church for Christ. He fears they will be led from their haplotes, their simple and sincere devotion to Christ, as Eve was deceived. And he names the intruders plainly as pseudapostolos, false apostles, counterfeits who only masquerade as apostles of Christ.
basic.typology: The betrothal of the church as a pure virgin to one husband fulfills the Old Testament picture of God as the husband of His people and looks ahead to the marriage of the Lamb. The deception of Eve becomes the pattern of every seduction from the truth, and the serpent behind it is unmasked as Satan still at work through false teachers.
basic.christ: Christ is the one husband to whom the church is betrothed, the pure and jealous love of the whole passage. He is the true Jesus whom the false teachers counterfeit with a different Jesus. The gospel Paul guards is the gospel of the real Christ, freely given, over against every disguised distortion that would rob the church of Him.
basic.god: God is the one whose jealousy Paul shares, the God who will not share His people's devotion with idols or impostors. He knows Paul's love, verse 11, and He stands behind the truth of Christ. The passage reveals a God who is at war with Satan's counterfeits and who will bring the deceivers to an end that matches their deeds.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 3 records the serpent's deception of Eve, which Paul makes his warning. Galatians 1 pronounces a curse on any different gospel. Ephesians 5 pictures Christ and the church as husband and bride. Revelation 19 shows the marriage of the Lamb to His pure bride.
basic.oneStory: Scripture tells of God betrothing a people to Himself and guarding them against the serpent's lies. Paul stands in that story as the friend of the Bridegroom, jealous to present the church as a pure virgin to Christ. The counterfeit gospel is the serpent's old work in new disguise, and the story runs toward the day when the true Bridegroom receives His spotless bride.

context.literary:
Chapters 10 to 13 are the hard edge of the letter, and chapter 11 is where the argument turns from defence to unmasking. The passage is built on three movements that share one concern: whose voice the Corinthians will listen to. Verses 1 to 6 are a pastoral appeal wrapped in a marriage image. Verses 7 to 12 are an argument from money, a defence of why Paul will not be paid. Verses 13 to 15 are the verdict, delivered in three short sentences that each rest on the one before: such men are false apostles, Satan is himself a counterfeit, therefore his servants are counterfeits too.

Paul writes in sustained irony. He asks to be borne with in a little 'foolishness,' verse 1, and then says the Corinthians are 'already doing that,' a gentle jab at how readily they tolerate showmen. He calls his rivals 'super-apostles' in verse 5, a label he picks up, probably from the Corinthians' own mouths, and then repeats in 12:11 to show how little he thinks of it. The questions in verses 7, 11 and 12 are rhetorical and expect the Corinthians to answer for themselves. The word 'masquerading' appears three times in verses 13 to 15, a drumbeat that makes disguise the point of the whole paragraph.

The hinge is verse 3, where Paul quietly turns a wedding into a garden. The language of betrothal in verse 2 is Old Testament covenant language; the language of the serpent and Eve in verse 3 is Genesis 3. Together they say that the church stands at the moment between promise and consummation, and that this is exactly the moment a serpent chooses to speak.

In the book's larger shape, this passage opens the 'fool's speech' that runs from 11:1 to 12:13. Paul has already announced in chapter 10 that he will not boast beyond his limit, and in 10:12 he said he would not compare himself with those who commend themselves. Here, forced against his will, he does what he said he would not do, and he says so repeatedly so that no one mistakes it for his real manner.
context.historical:
Corinth was a Roman colony, refounded in 44 BC, wealthy from trade between two harbours, and proud of its rhetoric. Public speakers, often called sophists, travelled from city to city selling their skill. They gave polished performances, collected fees, and attached themselves to wealthy patrons who protected them and received their praise. A teacher who took no money was easy to think of as a teacher worth little. This is the background to Paul's remark in verse 6 that he is not a polished speaker and to the sting behind his questions in verses 7 to 9. Paul had founded the church there, staying a year and a half, Acts 18:11, and supporting himself by tentmaking alongside Aquila and Priscilla, Acts 18:3. In 2 Corinthians 10:10 we hear what his critics said: his letters are weighty but his bodily presence is unimpressive and his speech of no account.

The rivals appear to be outsiders who arrived with letters of commendation, 3:1, and who stressed Jewish credentials, which is why Paul answers in verse 22 with 'Hebrews,' 'Israelites' and 'descendants of Abraham.' They probably claimed a status above Paul, hence 'super-apostles,' and they accepted payment from the Corinthians, which is why Paul says in verse 20 that they exploit them. Scholars debate whether they were the same people as the 'super-apostles,' who may be the Jerusalem leaders, or only their self-styled representatives. Paul's tone in 11:13 and the hint of 'another Jesus' in verse 4 point to the second reading, and Galatians 2:6 and 2:9 show Paul speaks respectfully of the Jerusalem pillars elsewhere.

The money issue was not a petty one. In Paul's world a teacher who accepted the Corinthians' support became their client, and a client does not rebuke his patron. By refusing it, Paul kept the freedom to speak plainly. He received help from Macedonia, verse 9, and Philippians 4:15 to 16 confirms that the Philippians sent gifts to him again and again. He defends the principle of support in 1 Corinthians 9:12 but declines to use the right for the sake of the gospel.
context.canonical:
The Old Testament lies under this passage on three levels. The first is the marriage of God and His people. The prophets speak of the LORD as husband and Israel as wife: 'For your husband is your Maker,' Isaiah 54:5, and 'I will betroth you to Me forever,' Hosea 2:19. The same prophets speak of Israel's unfaithfulness as adultery, Ezekiel 16. Paul takes that story and says the church now stands in Israel's place as the bride, and that he has given her away.

The second level is Genesis 3. Paul says Eve was deceived, using the same Greek verb, exapatao, that Paul uses in 1 Timothy 2:14. Notably he does not say Adam or Eve sinned through lust or defiance but through losing 'simple and pure devotion.' The serpent's method was not to propose an atheist replacement for God but to offer a better version of God's word. That is the template of the false teacher.

The third level is the Old Testament law of false prophets. Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5 allows for a prophet who performs signs yet leads the people to follow other gods, and commands Israel not to listen. Signs do not validate a message that contradicts the covenant God has given. Paul applies the same test to 'a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed.'

In the New Testament the warning recurs. Jesus warns of false prophets in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15. Paul curses any gospel contrary to the one he preached, even if it comes from an angel from heaven, Galatians 1:8 to 9. John tells believers to test the spirits, 1 John 4:1, and Peter predicts false teachers who exploit with deceptive words, 2 Peter 2:1 to 3. In Revelation 2:2 the church at Ephesus is commended for testing those who falsely claim to be apostles. The marriage image resolves in Ephesians 5:25 to 27 and in the wedding of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7 to 8, where the bride is clothed in fine linen and is finally presented.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant the Corinthians to feel the danger before they could argue about it. The marriage image is chosen to move them from a debate about credentials to a question of loyalty. A bride who is courted by another man in her betrothal period has a decision to make, and so do they. He wants them to see that the question is not whether the newcomers are impressive, eloquent or Jewish enough, but whether what they preach is the same Jesus, the same Spirit and the same gospel Corinth received at the start, verse 4.

He also meant them to see the money question rightly. His refusal of support was not coldness or an admission that his work was worth little. It was love, a deliberate choice to make the gospel free and to keep himself from being owned. And it was strategy, verse 12, to deny the intruders the claim that they work on the same terms as he does.

Finally, Paul intends to take away the intruders' most dangerous defence, which is that they look right. If Satan can look like an angel of light, appearance proves nothing. The Corinthians are therefore sent back to content: the Christ proclaimed, the Spirit received, the gospel accepted. Paul's authority rests on faithful proclamation of that content, not on style, and not on his own persuasiveness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records Paul's own practice and a judgment on particular people in a particular church. It describes his refusal of Corinthian support, but it does not make that refusal a law for all ministers. In 1 Corinthians 9:14 he says plainly that the Lord commanded that those who preach the gospel should get their living from the gospel, and he took gifts from Macedonia and Philippi. What carries forward is the principle behind the practice: a minister must not let money become a lever over the message.

The strong words of verses 13 to 15 are likewise a verdict on those who preached 'another Jesus,' not a licence to call every disagreeable teacher a servant of Satan. The test Paul applies is about the Christ proclaimed and the gospel received, not style, personality or ministry method. Believers are called to the same discernment with a gentle spirit, as in 1 John 4:1 and Galatians 6:1, and are not asked to read motives from the outside.

The marriage image applies directly to the church as a whole, and applies to the individual believer only through it. The present call is to single-hearted loyalty to Christ and a readiness to test every voice against the gospel already received.

debates.question: Who are the 'super-apostles' of verse 5, and are they the same as the false apostles of verse 13?

views.label: Two groups: the Jerusalem apostles and the intruders who invoked them
views.case: Paul calls the leaders of the Jerusalem church 'pillars' and speaks of them with respect in Galatians 2:9, and he says in 1 Corinthians 15:11 that he and they preach the same message. On this view the 'super-apostles' are the Twelve or their circle, whom Paul would not call false, and the false apostles are visitors who used their name to claim superiority.

views.label: One group of rivals
views.case: The tone of 11:5 and 12:11 is sarcastic and fits people Paul has no regard for. Verses 12 and 13 follow on directly, speaking of those who want to be regarded as 'our equals,' and the same people are called false apostles. On this view 'super-apostles' is the Corinthians' phrase, or the rivals' own, which Paul throws back with irony.

debates.bearing: Either way Paul's argument is the same: apostolic standing is judged by the gospel preached, not by status. If the first view is right, Paul's care to distinguish the false from the true shows he never attacks the Jerusalem leaders. If the second is right, the intruders are condemned by their message, not merely their manner. The passage does not require us to settle it.

debates.question: What was the false teaching: a different Jesus, or a different emphasis?

views.label: Jewish Christian legalism
views.case: Verse 22 stresses Hebrew descent, and the same letter has Paul writing about the old covenant and veil in chapter 3. Galatians shows a similar pressure to add Jewish observance to faith in Christ. On this reading the 'other Jesus' is a Messiah who needs the law's supplement.

views.label: A triumphalist, charismatic Christ
views.case: Paul's reply stresses weakness, vision, miracles and power, and he defends himself against charges of weak presence and speech. The rivals seem to have boasted in eloquence and spiritual experience and presented a Christ of glory without the cross. On this reading the other Jesus is a Jesus without suffering.

views.label: A combination, drawn from the letter's silence
views.case: Paul never lists the doctrines in dispute, only that the Jesus, the Spirit and the gospel differed. The silence may be intended: what matters is the pattern, not the particular heresy. Any message that replaces the crucified and risen Christ with a more attractive version fits.

debates.bearing: Whatever the content, the test is whether the message matches the Christ proclaimed from the start, verse 4. This keeps the warning usable for any age, in which the particular distortions change but the pattern of an attractive alternative persists.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's marriage language starts with a verb the basic text passes over. In verse 2 he says he 'promised' the church to one husband, from harmozo, a word that means to fit or join and is used of giving a woman in marriage. He speaks as the father of the bride who arranges the match, which matches 1 Corinthians 4:15, where he says that in Christ Jesus he became their father through the gospel. The verb carries a quiet implication: a match is made once, and the bride's task is to keep the promise.

In verse 3 the serpent's 'cunning' is panourgia, a word that means readiness to do anything, a skill with no moral limit. It is a general word for trickery elsewhere, Luke 20:23, Ephesians 4:14. The Greek Old Testament uses a different word for the serpent in Genesis 3:1, phronimos, a word that is positive in other places, so Paul chooses a sharper term to name what the shrewdness became. The echo is not accidental: in 12:16 Paul uses the related adjective panourgos of himself, quoting the charge that he was 'crafty' and caught the Corinthians by trickery. He takes the insult and turns it into irony.

The 'super-apostles' of verse 5 are hyperlian apostoloi, the adverb meaning 'exceedingly' or 'beyond measure.' The same compound appears in 12:11, and nowhere else in the New Testament. Paul does not say they are not apostles in this verse, only that he is not inferior. The verdict of 'false apostles' waits until verse 13, where the compound pseudapostoloi is formed.

In verse 6 Paul describes himself as an idiotes in speech, a word that originally meant a private person, one without professional training. It is the word used of Peter and John in Acts 4:13, where the BSB has 'ordinary men.' Paul accepts the label for his rhetoric but not for his knowledge, gnosis.

Verse 7 says he preached 'free of charge,' dorean, which is the same word used for grace in Romans 3:24 and for Jesus' command in Matthew 10:8, 'Freely you have received; freely give.' The gospel is given as a gift, and the messenger imitates the gift. 'Support' in verse 8 is opsonion, the word for a soldier's pay, Luke 3:14, 1 Corinthians 9:7. The verb he uses for taking it from other churches, sylao, means to strip or plunder, and it is clearly hyperbole: the Macedonian churches were willing givers, and Paul is being sarcastic about how the Corinthians would see it.

The last words of the passage sit on a verb used three times, metaschematizo, from schema, form or outward shape. Paul says the false apostles 'masquerade,' Satan himself 'masquerades,' and his servants also 'masquerade.' They change the outward form while the substance stays what it is. Their 'deceitful workers,' ergatai dolioi, in verse 13 sets labour against labour: Paul's work is exposed and honest, theirs is cunning.

typology.type: The bride betrothed and kept pure, Hosea 2:19 and Isaiah 54:5
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament pictured God as the husband of Israel and called her to faithfulness. Hosea has the LORD betrothing her again in righteousness, justice, loving devotion and faithfulness, and Isaiah says her husband is her Maker and Redeemer. Paul applies the picture to the church and himself as the one who arranged the match. The escalation in Christ is that the husband has given Himself up for His bride, Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and will present her without blemish at the wedding of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7 to 8. The type falls short in that Israel was a nation, but the church is drawn from every nation and cleansed by His blood, not by her own faithfulness.

typology.type: Eve and the serpent in Eden, Genesis 3:1 to 6
typology.fulfillment: Paul reads the garden story as the pattern for every seduction of the Lord's people. The serpent questioned God's word, softened its warning and offered a better version of the good. The false teachers at Corinth do the same with another Jesus and another gospel. The correspondence is not allegory; Paul does not say that the apostles are the serpent in any detail but that the method is the same. Christ is the escalation: He met the same tempter and answered with Scripture, Matthew 4:1 to 11. The type also falls short, because Eve's deception had unrepeatable cosmic consequences, while the Corinthians still have time to return.

typology.type: The false prophet who performs signs, Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5
typology.fulfillment: Moses told Israel that a prophet might give a sign that came true and yet lead them to other gods, and that Israel must not listen, because the LORD was testing them. The signs did not authenticate the message. Paul's refusal to rest his claim on style or credentials follows the same pattern, and his appeal to the Christ proclaimed from the start is the New Testament form of Israel's rule to hold to the covenant word. The fulfilment in Christ is that the true prophet has come, the Son who speaks the Father's words, Hebrews 1:1 to 2, and He is the standard by which every later teacher is tested. The parallel falls short in that Moses spoke of a test of love for the LORD, while Paul speaks of an attack on the one Mediator who has come.

typology.type: The priests' portion and the free gospel, Numbers 18:21 and 1 Corinthians 9:13
typology.fulfillment: Under the law the priests lived from the altar and the Levites from the tithe, Numbers 18:21, a practice Paul mentions in 1 Corinthians 9:13. Paul's refusal of Corinth's support is no rejection of that principle, but a choice to make the gospel visible as a gift. The correspondence in Christ is that He gave without charge: 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve,' Mark 10:45. Paul's practice mirrors that pattern in small. The type falls short at the obvious point, that Paul's giving cannot atone for anyone; it only displays the gift already given by Christ.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ by naming Him as the husband at the heart of the church's life. The 'one husband' of verse 2 is Christ, and Paul's whole pastoral aim is to present a church to Him that is undivided in love. Elsewhere the aim of Christ's saving work is stated in the same terms: He loved the church and gave Himself up for her, to present her to Himself holy and blameless, Ephesians 5:25 to 27. So Paul's jealousy is derived from Christ's. He does not want the church for himself, only for the Lord who loved her first.

It leads to Christ by naming the content of the gospel as a person. The sin Paul fears is not a lapse of manners but receiving 'a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed.' This shows how much the gospel depends on who Jesus is. A different Jesus is a different salvation. The Christ of Scripture is the crucified and risen Lord, Son of God, and Servant, and every substitute either removes the cross, as the triumphalist version does, or adds to it, as the legal version does. Paul will spend the next chapters showing that the true Christ is known through suffering and weakness, 11:23 to 33, and 12:9 to 10, which is why the rival Jesus is a Jesus without a cross.

It leads to Christ by pattern, for Paul's refusal of payment imitates the Lord who gave without price. 'I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge,' he says, using the language of grace. The apostle makes himself low so that the church may be lifted up, verse 7, which is exactly the movement of Philippians 2:5 to 8 and of Mark 10:45. The humbling and exalting of verse 7 is a miniature of the incarnation: He, who is rich, became poor, so that we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9.

It leads to Christ by contrast with the false apostles. They exploit, enslave and put on a show; Christ is the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. The hired hand runs when the wolf comes, John 10:12, but Paul says he fears for the flock, and Jesus warned that the wolves would come in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15. Counterfeits prove that there is a real coin. The fact that Satan counterfeits an angel of light implies the existence of true light, and Jesus says 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The passage does not turn every detail into a picture of Jesus; the point is not that Paul is Christ, but that he is a servant who points away from himself. Christ's own words to the church at Ephesus, who tested the false apostles, Revelation 2:2, show that He cares about this discernment. And the end of the story is a wedding where the bride, once at risk of being led astray, stands in fine linen before her Husband, Revelation 19:7 to 8.
study.god:
The God of this passage is first of all a jealous God. The word 'jealousy' is used of Him in the commandments, Exodus 20:5, and it is not a flaw. It is the love of a husband who will not share a wife, and it is the other side of covenant faithfulness. Paul shares it 'with a godly jealousy,' which means it comes from God and aims at God's own purpose. The jealousy of a good husband and the jealousy of a spurned rival are different things, and Paul's is the first. It is a love that wants the beloved to be safe.

God is also the one who has made the betrothal. Paul says 'I promised you to one husband,' but the underlying work is God's: He called them in Christ, and He will present them. The apostle is the one who arranges the introduction; the Lord is the one who arranges the marriage. That puts a sober note on the church's life. She is not her own, and her loyalty is not a matter of preference but of promise.

God knows. 'God knows I do!' says Paul in verse 11, appealing to the one witness who can see Paul's heart. This matters because the Corinthians cannot verify his motives, and the rivals have made suspicion their business. The God who knows hearts is also the one before whom the false apostles will stand, for 'their end will correspond to their actions,' verse 15. There is justice in this: the end of a counterfeit is to be exposed, and the God of truth is not mocked.

The passage also shows a God who is sovereign over deception without being its author. Satan can masquerade as an angel of light, but he does so under limits. The same letter says in 4:4 that the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, and in 2:11 that believers are not unaware of his schemes. The Scripture does not make evil a rival god. It presents Satan as a creature who counterfeits what belongs to God, and who cannot create light, only imitate it.

God is also gracious in how He guards His people. He gives them a warning before the damage is done. Paul's letter is an act of divine care: 'I am afraid,' he says, which is a pastor's way of saying that God has put this on his heart. The Corinthians have the Spirit they received, the Christ they heard and the gospel they believed, and each is a safeguard.

For worship, the passage invites a clean heart. If God is a jealous husband, the right response is not anxiety but undivided devotion, a love that is simple and pure. And it sets a standard for those who lead in His name: to be free of money's hold, to seek people and not their possessions, and to speak the truth before the God who knows.

crossReferences.note: The story Paul has in mind in verse 3. The serpent begins with a question about what God said, and ends by offering something better than God's gift. Paul sees the same shape in the Corinthian crisis: not open rejection of Christ but a more attractive version of Him.

The Lord promises to betroth Israel to Himself forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion and faithfulness. The language of covenant betrothal stands behind Paul's picture of the church as a bride promised to one husband, and shows that the marriage is God's initiative and God's faithfulness.

Israel's husband is her Maker and Redeemer. Paul uses the same picture and extends it to a church that includes Gentiles. The husband is the covenant God who has acted to save, which is why divided loyalty is so serious.

A prophet who works signs but leads the people after other gods must not be heeded. The test is the covenant message, not the miracle. Paul applies the same principle to those who proclaim another Jesus and expects the Corinthians to apply it.

Paul pronounces a curse on any gospel contrary to the one he preached, even from an angel from heaven. It strengthens verse 14 of our passage: even a being that looks like an angel of light has no authority to change the message. The same sharpness appears in both letters.

Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to present her glorious and without blemish. Paul's jealousy in 2 Corinthians 11:2 anticipates this goal and is its pastoral side: he works so that Christ will find His bride faithful.

The marriage of the Lamb has come and the bride is ready in fine linen. This is where the betrothal of 2 Corinthians 11:2 ends, at a wedding rather than a warning. The danger of deception is real only because the promise it threatens is so great.

Paul explains that he has a right to support but does not use it, enduring anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ. It shows that his refusal in 2 Corinthians 11:7 to 9 is a considered policy, not a lack of regard for ministers' support.

The Philippians partnered with Paul in giving and receiving, again and again, and he calls their gift a fragrant offering. This is the kind of support Paul accepts, support that is a free gift and not a purchase of influence. It matches the 'brothers from Macedonia' of 2 Corinthians 11:9.

The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so that they cannot see the light of the gospel. It gives the background to 11:14: the enemy works as a counterfeit of light because the true light is the gospel of Christ's glory, and he cannot bear it to shine.

The church at Ephesus is praised for testing those who claim to be apostles and exposing them as liars. This is the discernment Paul asks of the Corinthians, and it shows that Christ Himself expects His church to test the claims of those who speak in His name.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden in which a man and woman walk with God, and a voice that asks whether God's word can be trusted. This passage sees that old scene replayed in a Greek port city. The question of Genesis 3:1, 'Did God really say?', has a descendant in verse 4 of our passage, where someone proclaims 'a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed.' The story of Scripture is, among other things, the story of how God's people are drawn away from a simple devotion and brought back to it.

The prophets continue the story. Israel is the bride of the LORD, and she is unfaithful, Hosea 2:2 and Ezekiel 16, and the LORD promises to betroth her again forever, Hosea 2:19. The New Testament announces that this has happened in Christ, who gave Himself for her, and that the church now stands as the betrothed bride. Paul is the friend of the bridegroom, to use John the Baptist's picture from John 3:29, who prepares the bride and guards her until the wedding. He does not wish to be her husband; he wishes to hand her over pure.

The passage also touches the thread of the false prophet that runs through the whole canon. Israel was warned about prophets who would lead her astray, Deuteronomy 13, and the history of the kings is full of voices that told the king what he wished to hear, 1 Kings 22. Jesus warns of wolves in sheep's clothing, Paul of 'savage wolves' in Acts 20:29, and Peter of false teachers who exploit, 2 Peter 2:1 to 3. Revelation then names the great deceiver of the nations, Revelation 12:9 and 20:10. The counterfeit angel of light in 2 Corinthians 11:14 belongs to that line and is finally unmasked.

Finally, the passage looks forward to the day the story ends. The church that is now at risk of being led astray will be presented, and the long drama of unfaithfulness and fidelity will conclude in a wedding. 'His bride has made herself ready,' says Revelation 19:7, and the one who stood outside the garden in exile will see the city where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:2 to 3. Until then the call remains the one Paul gives: keep your mind on the Christ who was proclaimed, and trust that the one who promised you to Himself will bring the promise home.

quiz.q: Why is Paul jealous for the Corinthians with a godly jealousy?

options.text: Because he betrothed them to one husband, Christ, and wants to present them pure to Him.
options.note: Verse 2 gives the marriage imagery behind Paul's jealousy.

options.text: Because he wants them loyal to himself rather than other teachers.
options.note: His jealousy is for Christ, not for his own following.

options.text: Because he envies the success of the other apostles.
options.note: This is a godly jealousy for the church, not sinful envy.
Money is not the issue in his jealousy; devotion to Christ is.

quiz.q: What does Paul fear will happen to the Corinthians, and by what example?

options.text: That their minds will be led astray from pure devotion to Christ, as Eve was deceived.
options.note: Verse 3 compares the danger to the serpent's deception of Eve.

options.text: That they will simply grow bored with the gospel over time.
options.note: The danger is active seduction by deceivers, not mere boredom.

options.text: That they will face persecution and give up.
options.note: The threat here is deception, not persecution.

options.text: That they will become too generous with their money.
options.note: The concern is spiritual seduction from Christ, not generosity.

quiz.q: Why did Paul preach the gospel to the Corinthians free of charge?

options.text: To humble himself and exalt them, being no burden, unlike the money-seeking rivals.
options.note: Verses 7 to 9 show Paul refusing support to serve them freely.

options.text: Because the gospel has no real value worth paying for.
options.note: He preached free of charge out of love, not because the gospel lacked worth.

options.text: Because he was independently wealthy and needed nothing.
options.note: He was in need, but Macedonian brothers supplied him.

options.text: Because he was forbidden to accept any money at all.
options.note: He did accept support from other churches; this was his choice for Corinth.

quiz.q: How does Paul unmask the false apostles in verses 13 to 15?

options.text: As deceitful workers and servants of Satan, who masquerades as an angel of light.
options.note: Paul exposes their true master behind the disguise of righteousness.

options.text: As sincere but poorly trained teachers.
options.note: Paul calls them frauds, not merely undertrained.

options.text: As rivals who simply have a different style.
options.note: The issue is not style but a counterfeit gospel and false allegiance.
Paul warns they are dangerous servants of Satan whose end matches their deeds.

questions: Paul is jealous to present the church as a pure virgin to Christ. What would single-hearted, undivided devotion to Christ look like in your own life right now?
Paul fears the Corinthians will be deceived as Eve was. What subtle teachings or cultural pressures are drawing your heart from simple devotion to Christ?
A different Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel can be received very easily. How do you test what you hear against the true gospel Paul preached?
Paul refused pay so he would be no burden and his motives would be clear. Where might your own generosity or restraint make the gospel more believable to others?
Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, and false teaching often looks righteous. How can you grow in discernment without becoming cynical or suspicious of everyone?

translationNotes.note: Godly jealousy translates a phrase meaning the jealousy of God; the word zelos can be sinful envy or, as here, a holy, protective ardor for the church's fidelity to Christ.
Simple and pure devotion renders haplotes, singleness or sincerity of heart; some manuscripts add and purity, but the sense is an undivided attachment to Christ.
Super-apostles is Paul's ironic title for his opponents, kept in curly quotation marks as in the BSB to signal the sarcasm.
False apostles renders pseudapostolos, a term Paul coins for counterfeit sent ones; masquerading translates a word for disguising or transforming oneself in outward appearance.
